newsitem.title: USA: U.S. voters send states mixed message on taxes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. voters send states mixed message on taxes.

text.p: Voters sent state officials a conflicting message Tuesday on their willingness to countenance tax increases, approving measures to restrict tax policy in some states but rejecting similar plans in others.
Voters in California, Florida, Nevada and South Dakota okayed ballot initiatives that will make it more difficult for state officials to increase their taxes.
But in Idaho, Nebraska and Oregon, measures that would have increased restrictions on tax hikes went down to defeat.

"It does look as if it is a mixed bag," said Michael Johnston, head of municipal research at Sandler O'Neill & Partners. Johnston said one explanation may lie in voters' differing perceptions of their own economic well-being.

"Whenever the economy is really bad there's a greater momentum for people to vote in favor of tax limitation measures," he said. "But when the economy is doing well, it's not that those feelings go away, but they become less important."

One of the most closely watched tax initiatives was California's Proposition 218, which requires voter approval for new taxes and property-related fees. The measure also gives voters the right to end existing taxes by voting them down in a referendum.
Despite warnings from Wall Street that the plan would hurt local credit quality, California voters gave it a strong endorsement, approving the measure by almost 13 percentage points.

Richard Raphael, executive managing director at Fitch Investors Service Inc, said approval of the California initiative reflects a trend toward placing more obstacles in the way of state fiscal managers.
"It seems to be an expansion of this whole process of shifting control to taxpayers and taking away flexibility of the governmental entity," Raphael said.
In contrast to the California result, voters in Idaho soundly rejected a measure that would have placed limits on property taxes there.
The Idaho plan, which would have restricted local governments' ability to raise property taxes to one percent of the assessed value of taxable property, was opposed by 63 percent of the electorate.
Jerry Caden, an credit analyst at Moody's Investors Service Inc, said the Idaho measure would have cut $75 million from city and county coffers, and about $228 million from local school districts.
The result was the opposite in Florida, where voters approved a measure requiring two-thirds voter approval for statewide tax increases imposed via constitutional amendment.
The effect of the vote will be to make it more difficult to impose an income tax in the state, which is already prohibited by the state constitution.
"I think it's a pretty strong political statement that people don't want to pay more taxes," Barbara Flickinger, a Moody's analysts who watches local Florida credits, said.
But Flickinger said the effect on revenues will be negligible. The state Legislature can still raise sales taxes, which make up 80 percent of tax revenues already, she said.

"It doesn't really restrict the state's flexibility." Oregon voters rejected a measure that would have required tax and revenue increases be approved by a majority of all registered voters, instead of just a majority of people who show up to vote. A companion initiative to cut property taxes and cap future growth was judged too close to call late Wednesday.

South Dakota voters approved a plan to require either voter approval or a super-majority -- a two-thirds vote -- by the Legislature to raise existing taxes or institute new ones. Nevada voters also decided to make it more difficult for lawmakers to raise taxes, approving an initiative requiring a super-majority vote of two-thirds in both houses of the Legislature to raise revenues.
In Nebraska, voters defeated a plan to place additional limits on property tax increases. Analysts warned that approval of the measure would have cost about $400 million in lost revenues annually.
REUTER
